questions.q: Per this lesson, what is The Graph relative to the listen/write/query pattern established earlier in the chapter?
options: One well-built, widely adopted implementation of that pattern — not the only possible one
The only valid way to implement the pattern; custom indexers don't follow it
A replacement for the pattern entirely, using a different architecture
A tool unrelated to indexing, used only for wallet authentication
questions.explain: The lesson frames The Graph explicitly as one implementation among options, with a self-built custom indexer as the honest alternative following the same underlying pattern.

questions.q: What four things does this lesson say a managed service like The Graph gives you for free that you'd otherwise build yourself?
options: Indexing infrastructure, an auto-generated GraphQL query layer, a public directory (Graph Explorer), and decentralized redundancy
Unlimited free production query volume with no billing model at all
A guarantee that any business logic, including third-party API calls, can run inside a handler
Full control over the exact SQL schema used to store indexed data
questions.explain: The lesson lists these four specific benefits of the managed path, each paired with what you'd otherwise have to operate yourself.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what kind of handler logic does a subgraph's determinism constraint rule out?
options: Calling out to a third-party API mid-handler, or any logic needing non-chain, non-deterministic inputs
Reading any field from the event object that triggered the handler
Saving more than one entity per handler invocation
Using BigInt or Bytes types anywhere in a mapping
questions.explain: The lesson ties this back to Lesson 14's determinism requirement — handlers can't call external APIs or use anything non-deterministic.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe a custom indexer, in terms of earlier chapter content?
options: Chapter 2's event listener, extended with your own database schema and your own API layer, that you operate and scale yourself
A completely different architecture that doesn't use event listening at all
A paid upgrade tier within Subgraph Studio itself
A tool that only works for contracts that don't emit any events
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly defines a custom indexer as Lesson 10's listener service extended with your own storage and API, run on your own infrastructure.

questions.q: What does the lesson recommend as a common, reasonable pattern rather than a sign of indecision?
options: Using a subgraph for public, reusable data while running a custom indexer for internal, proprietary queries — both at once
Always choosing a custom indexer regardless of the use case, since it offers more control
Never publishing a subgraph publicly, even for data meant to be shared
Switching between managed and custom indexing on a monthly rotation
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls out running both a public subgraph and an internal custom indexer side by side as a common, sensible split rather than indecision.
